stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .07", Sentence = "There was weak evidence for callousness negatively moderating cheap talk, though the credible interval included zero (β = -.05, p = .07, 95% CI [-.13, .02])."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Cooperative behavior is often viewed as evidence of altruistic motivation.
Yet, cost-free, non-binding signals of intended cooperation -known as cheap talk -can also shape others' future behavior to one's advantage.
Distinguishing unconditional altruistic cooperation from this more strategic cooperative signaling is difficult experimentally, because the same action can reflect either motive.

We present a modified trust game that dissociates these motivations by allowing participants to emit cost-free cooperative signals that neither alter immediate payoffs nor commit them to future cooperation, but that could encourage future investments.

In three online samples of adults (n = 253 / 488 / 827), participants learned to use cheap talk strategically, signaling greater willingness to cooperate when doing so could encourage future investment.
Overall, exploitativeness, a facet of antagonism, positively predicted cheap talk, whereas callousness and aggression showed weaker, negative associations.
Cooperative behavior therefore serves not only as an expression of altruistic motivation, but also as a strategic tool for shaping others' expectations and future choices.
More broadly, these findings demonstrate how the social-cognitive capacities that sustain human cooperation can also be deployed instrumentally to influence others.
Cooperation is fundamental to human social life, allowing people to form relationships, coordinate their behavior, and pursue shared goals.
Yet, cooperative behavior does not always reflect cooperative motives.
Consider a new colleague who goes out of their way to help you with an important project.
The gesture appears generous, but is it necessarily so?
They may genuinely wish to help, feel bound by social norms, or be cultivating trust in anticipation of needing your assistance later.
In each case, the behavior is identical, but the underlying motivation differs dramatically.

This ambiguity reflects a fundamental challenge in understanding human cooperation: cooperative acts strongly influence our decisions about whom to trust, yet those acts may themselves be shaped by an interest in appearing trustworthy.

When deciding whom to trust, assist, transact with, and select as future interaction partners, people often look to past cooperative behavior (Allen et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2010; FeldmanHall et al., 2018).
text.formatted: When deciding whom to trust, assist, transact with, and select as future interaction partners, people often look to past cooperative behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chang et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">FeldmanHall et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the evolutionary mechanisms of direct and indirect reciprocity, reputation-based cooperation, and partner choice all depend on individuals' tracking others' cooperative behavior and using it to guide subsequent decisions (Nowak & Sigmund, 2005; Trivers, 1971).
text.formatted: Indeed, the evolutionary mechanisms of direct and indirect reciprocity, reputation-based cooperation, and partner choice all depend on individuals' tracking others' cooperative behavior and using it to guide subsequent decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Nowak & Sigmund, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Trivers, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: From the actor's perspective, this creates an incentive to behave cooperatively when doing so can shape how others behave in future interactions.

Consistent with this perspective, people cooperate more in experiments when their actions are observable, carry reputational consequences, or affect access to future opportunities (Barclay & Willer, 2006; Fehr & Fischbacher, 2003; Milinski et al., 2002; Wedekind & Milinski, 2000).

text.text: Thus, cooperation functions not only as an allocation of resources, but also as a way to shape a partner's future behavior.
For a cooperative signal to be useful, however, others must find it credible.

Signaling theory (Spence, 1973) proposes that costs help to maintain credibility by making them more difficult -or less worthwhile -to produce for people who lack the quality or intention being signaled (Gintis et al., 2001; Grafen, 1990; Smith & Harper, 2003).
text.formatted: Signaling theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Spence, 1973)</ref> proposes that costs help to maintain credibility by making them more difficult -or less worthwhile -to produce for people who lack the quality or intention being signaled <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gintis et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Grafen, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Smith & Harper, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: For example, staying late to finish a task with a colleague is stronger evidence of cooperativeness than simply offering to help because staying late requires giving up personal time -a cost that only a truly cooperative person would typically be willing to bear.
Not all social signals are costly, however.
Merely offering to help your colleague (without actually doing so) can foster an impression of cooperativeness without requiring any immediate sacrifice.
In game theory, cost-free, nonbinding communication is often described as cheap talk (Crawford & Sobel, 1982; Farrell & Rabin, 1996).
text.formatted: In game theory, cost-free, nonbinding communication is often described as cheap talk <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crawford & Sobel, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Farrell & Rabin, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Because cheap talk neither alters immediate payoffs nor commits the sender to subsequent behavior, it can easily be used to claim cooperative intentions that the sender does not actually hold.

Nevertheless, sender-receiver models show that cheap talk can convey information when the parties' interests are at least partially aligned -for example, when both colleagues benefit from a productive relationship (Crawford & Sobel, 1982).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, sender-receiver models show that cheap talk can convey information when the parties' interests are at least partially aligned -for example, when both colleagues benefit from a productive relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crawford & Sobel, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: As interests diverge, however, cheap talk becomes less informative because the sender has more to gain by misrepresenting their intentions.
Cheap talk can therefore communicate genuine cooperative intentions, but it can also be used strategically to cultivate trust and encourage favorable treatment.
Critically, the tendency to use cooperative signals as cheap talk should vary across individuals.

In dimensional models of personality and psychopathology, agreeableness-antagonism captures individuals' ability to align their goals with those of others and sustain positive social relationships (DeYoung, 2015; Lynam & Miller, 2019).
text.formatted: In dimensional models of personality and psychopathology, agreeableness-antagonism captures individuals' ability to align their goals with those of others and sustain positive social relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(DeYoung, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lynam & Miller, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Across classic economic games and real-world contexts, self-reported agreeableness predicts more cooperative, prosocial, and forgiving behavior, whereas antagonism is typically associated with selfishness, defection, and conflict (Carlo et al., 2005; Habashi et al., 2016; Yarkoni et al., 2015; Zhao & Smillie, 2015).

text.text: Factor analyses distinguish at least three related facets of agreeableness-antagonism: compassion v. callousness, which contrasts empathy and altruism with a lack of concern for others, pacifism v. aggression, which contrasts nonviolence and conflict avoidance with aggression, and politeness v. exploitativeness, which contrasts honesty and humility with dishonesty, selfishness, and grandiosity (Allen et al., 2017; Crowe et al., 2018; Sleep et al., 2021).

text.text: These facets exhibit divergent social cognition profiles.

For example, callousness and aggression are typically associated with poorer performance on classic theory of mind or mentalization tasks, whereas exploitativeness is associated with better performance (Allen et al., 2017; Blain et al., 2021 Blain et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: For example, callousness and aggression are typically associated with poorer performance on classic theory of mind or mentalization tasks, whereas exploitativeness is associated with better performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Allen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Blain et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Blain et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: This divergence also extends to social learning.

Using a modified repeated trust game, we found that learning signals tracking how well participants anticipated a partner's cooperative behavior were weaker among individuals higher in callousness and aggression but stronger among more exploitative individuals.
These findings suggest callousness and aggression reflect reduced sensitivity to cooperation incentives, whereas exploitativeness is linked to more effective learning about others' behavior.
These individual differences may also have consequences for the use of cheap talk.

Cheap talk separates the benefits of appearing cooperative from the costs of committing to cooperation, making it potentially attractive to individuals who are both inclined to use others instrumentally and particularly adept at predicting how others will interpret and respond to one's behavior.
Thus, exploitative individuals should be particularly prone to using cooperative cheap talk to influence social partners, whereas callous and aggressive individuals may be less inclined to do so.
A central obstacle in cooperation research is that identical cooperative acts can arise from fundamentally different psychological processes.

In many experimental paradigms, the same action can both benefit another person and influence how the actor is perceived or treated in the future, making altruistic and strategic motives difficult to disentangle (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?nYsbHD  Bourgeois-Gironde & Corcos, 2011; Snijder et al., 2026).

text.text: For example, in repeated trust games, reciprocating an investment both benefits the investor immediately and may encourage greater trust on subsequent interactions (King-Casas et al., 2005 , 2008).

text.text: Similarly, in reputation-and partner-choice paradigms, cooperative acts simultaneously benefit others and improve one's reputation or access to desirable partners (Fehrler & Przepiorka, 2016; Milinski et al., 2002; Serdarevic et al., 2021).

text.text: This same ambiguity characterized our own prior trust game studies: participants' cooperative choices reflected learning from a partner's past behavior, but the underlying motive -strategic influence, norm adherence, or unconditional altruismremained unclear (Allen et al., 2024; Vanyukov et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This same ambiguity characterized our own prior trust game studies: participants' cooperative choices reflected learning from a partner's past behavior, but the underlying motive -strategic influence, norm adherence, or unconditional altruismremained unclear <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Vanyukov et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To address this limitation, we developed a multi-round trust paradigm that distinguishes cooperative cheap talk from costly cooperation.
In a standard trust game, cooperation by the trustee is costly: returning part of an investment benefits the investor but reduces the trustee's immediate payoff.
Our task manipulates this cost while holding the expressed cooperative intention constant.
In one condition, participants decide whether to return an investment before learning whether the investor shared it, meaning that their decision may carry monetary consequences.
In another, participants whose partner has already declined to invest indicate whether they would have returned the investment had it been shared.

This counterfactual response is communicated to the partner but cannot alter the participant's immediate payoff or commit them to future cooperation; it therefore constitutes cheap talk in the game-theoretic sense.
Critically, observing cheap talk alone cannot reveal whether it reflects strategic signaling or a general tendency to cooperate.
A general preference for cooperation will promote both cost-free expressions of willingness to cooperate and cooperation that carries actual costs.

We therefore operationalize individual differences in cooperative cheap talk as the extent to which people selectively express cooperation when it is cost-free relative to when it is costly -a pattern consistent with strategic signaling.
Manipulating partner reciprocity additionally allowed us to examine whether the use of cheap talk varied with the partner's responsiveness to cooperative signals.
The present study leverages this new paradigm to ask whether people strategically use cooperative cheap talk to influence others, and whether this behavior varies across facets of antagonism.
We first tested whether participants expressed greater willingness to cooperate when doing so was cost-free and nonbinding, but could plausibly encourage future investment.
We also examined whether cheap talk varied with the partner's reciprocity, which could affect the perceived value of attempting to influence that partner.
Finally, building on our prior findings, we hypothesized that exploitativeness would predict greater cheap talk, reflecting a propensity to use cooperative signals instrumentally.
In contrast, aggression and callousness were expected to predict reduced cheap talk, reflecting either diminished concern for social coordination or reduced sensitivity to social contingencies.

text.formatted: The Cooperative Signaling Task (CST; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) is a 222-trial modified trust game designed to assess the strategic use of cost-free cooperative signals (i.e., cheap talk) to influence a partner's future behavior.

text.text: Participants play as trustees ("leprechauns") interacting with three ostensible investors ("merchants") who reciprocate at fixed rates (75%, 50%, or 25%, otherwise responding randomly).
On each trial, the investor receives one gold coin and decides whether to keep or share it.
If shared, the coin is multiplied (1×, 3×, or 5×; randomly assigned), and the participant chooses whether to return half or keep the full amount.
The multiplier is revealed only after the participant's decision, preventing conditioning on payoff magnitude and dissociating expectations about the investor's behavior from monetary outcomes.
Participants complete three runs of two block types that differ in the timing of information.
In the Investment-Aware block (akin to the classic trust game), the investor's decision is revealed before the participant responds.
If the investor shares, the participant decides whether to return half or keep the multiplied amount.
If the investor keeps, participants indicate whether they would have returned had it been shared.
Because this response neither affects payoffs nor commits the participant to future cooperation, it constitutes cooperative cheap talk.
In the Investment-Blind block, participants decide whether to return before learning the investor's choice; if the investor shares, their precommitted decision is carried out.

Thus, in the Investment-Blind block, participants cannot condition their choice on the investor's immediate behavior, and return decisions provide a baseline index of general cooperativeness under uncertainty.

Our primary outcome, cheap talk, is operationalized as the interaction between block type and investor decision, indexing the extent to which the Investment-Aware versus Investment-Blind difference in return behavior is greater on investor-keep than investor-share trials.
Participants complete three runs, one per investor type; the 50% investor always comes first, with the 75-25% investors counterbalanced and block order randomized.
Participants are led to believe they are interacting with real partners.

The task is identical across samples except that Sample 3 did not include the 25% reciprocating investor (n trials = 148), and button placement was counterbalanced in Samples 2 and 3 to rule out response-side bias as a potential confound.
Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to evaluate whether selected scales were strong indicators of the latent constructs of callousness, aggression, and exploitativeness.

In the initial CFA model in Sample 1, Callousness was indicated by BFAS Compassion, IRI Perspective-Taking, IRI Empathic Concern, PID-5 Callousness, and ESI Lack of Empathy; Exploitativeness by PID-5 Manipulativeness, PID-5 Deceitfulness, PID-5 Grandiosity, PID-5 Attention-Seeking, and ESI Lack of Honesty; and Aggression by ESI Relational Aggression, ESI Physical Aggression, ESI Destructive Aggression, ESI Theft, and ESI Fraud.

Model fit for the CFA was determined using established criteria for acceptable and good fit: comparative fit index (CFI) ≥ .90/.95, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) ≤ .08/.06, and the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) ≤ .10/.08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Kline, 2016).

Adjustments (e.g., residual correlations) to the model were permitted only when theoretically defensible.

The final CFA model established in Sample 1 was specified identically in Samples 2 and 3.
Model fit and model adjustments were handled using the same criteria in all samples.

text.text: Within-person predictors included block (Aware versus Blind), investor decision (keep versus share), and their interaction (cheap talk).
We first examined models in which investor-type indicators were included as covariates, and then examined models where investor type was allowed to moderate cheap talk.
To account for task progression effects, models included centered within-block trial and global trial.
Each progression variable interacted with block, investor decision, and block × investor decision, allowing cheap talk to change both within blocks and across successive investors.
Models included a participant-specific random intercept and random slopes for all within-person predictors, with random effects allowed to correlate.
To examine personality moderation, latent factors representing callousness, exploitativeness, and aggression were included at the between-person level.
These traits were specified as simultaneous predictors of both the random intercept and slopes.
This specification allowed personality to moderate both cheap talk and its change over task progression.

By modeling random slopes as latent variables and integrating the measurement model directly into the structural model, this approach reduces measurement error and minimizes cross-level confounding, providing a rigorous test of whether antagonism facets account for individual differences in strategic cheap talk.

Note that Bayesian posterior probabilities quantify the extent to which the data support a given hypothesis, which allows for stronger inference than frequentist approaches that quantify the probability of observing the data under the null hypothesis.

text.text: Multilevel structural equation modeling was used to examine our hypothesis that participants would engage in cheap talk when given the opportunity to signal cooperation at no cost.

Cheap talk was operationalized as the within-person block × investor decision interaction predicting trial-level return decisions, with the expectation that return rates would be higher in the Investment-Aware block relative to the Investment-Blind block specifically on trials in which the investor kept.
In all three samples, the block × investor decision interaction was significant, indicating that the effect of block was contingent on the investor's behavior (Supplemental Table S7).
text.formatted: In all three samples, the block × investor decision interaction was significant, indicating that the effect of block was contingent on the investor's behavior (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: Probing this interaction revealed that when investors kept, participants returned at significantly higher rates in the Investment-Aware block relative to the Investment-Blind block.

Thus, participants selectively indicated willingness to cooperate in the Investment-Aware block, where return decisions on keep trials were cost-free, relative to the Investment-Blind block, where return decisions could entail monetary consequences (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: Thus, participants selectively indicated willingness to cooperate in the Investment-Aware block, where return decisions on keep trials were cost-free, relative to the Investment-Blind block, where return decisions could entail monetary consequences (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: In all samples, participants also returned less often in the Investment-Aware block relative to the Investment-Blind block when the investor had shared, consistent with greater temptation or cost salience once an investment is known.
There was a main effect of investor reciprocity, such that participants returned more with the 75% reciprocal investor than the 50% (all samples) or 25% (Samples 1 & 2) investor.
text.formatted: There was a main effect of investor reciprocity, such that participants returned more with the 75% reciprocal investor than the 50% (all samples) or 25% (Samples 1 & 2) investor.

text.text: Participants also returned less as the block progressed and, in Sample 1 only, as the task progressed.
Cheap talk increased both within each investor interaction, and as participants encountered subsequent investors, both of which are consistent with learning.
Separate Bayesian MSEMs showed no evidence that cheap talk varied by investor reciprocity in any sample (Table S8).

text.text: Taken together, these results represent strong evidence, across three independent samples, that participants selectively engaged in cheap talk, using cost-free cooperative signaling to plausibly influence their counterpart's future investment behavior.
To examine associations between antagonism and cheap talk at the latent level, we first established a three-factor measurement model that could be carried forward into structural analyses.

text.text: To test whether cheap talk varies as a function of antagonistic traits, we extended our original Bayesian MSEM by adding latent between-person callousness, aggression, and exploitativeness factors as predictors of heterogeneity in the random slopes in the model, including the within-person cheap talk effect (the slope for the block × investor decision interaction).
In Sample 1, consistent with our hypotheses, exploitativeness positively moderated the cheap talk effect (Figure 4).

text.text: In contrast, aggression was associated with reduced cheap talk, and there was no effect of callousness (see Table S9).

text.text: This pattern of findings replicated in Sample 3, where exploitativeness was again positively associated with cheap talk, aggression was negatively associated, and callousness showed no association.

Follow-up models allowing these trait effects to vary by investor reciprocity indicated that neither the positive association with Exploitativeness nor the negative association with Aggression differed across investor types in Samples 1 and 3 (Table S10).

text.text: Effects were weaker in Sample 2.
For exploitativeness, 85.1% of the posterior distribution lay above zero, falling short of the pre-specified 95% criterion, and providing only weak evidence for a positive association.
Aggression did not predict individual differences in cheap talk in Sample 2, whereas callousness negatively moderated the cheap talk effect.

This implies that participants at the lower pole of callousness -who were more empathic and compassionate -showed an increase in cooperative signaling from the Investment-Blind to the Investment-Aware block on investor-keep trials.
In follow-up analyses, we examined whether associations between antagonistic traits and cheap talk varied by investor reciprocity.
No significant moderation effects emerged in Sample 1.

In Sample 2, higher Callousness was associated with relatively less cheap talk with high-and low-reciprocating investors compared with medium-reciprocating investors, although neither investor-type contrast was significant overall.
In Sample 3, higher Exploitativeness attenuated the greater cheap talk observed with high-relative to medium-reciprocating investors (Table S10).

text.text: Thus, evidence for moderation by investor reciprocity was inconsistent across samples.
In sensitivity analyses probing the attenuated effect of exploitativeness on cheap talk behavior in Sample 2, we uncovered two contributing factors.
First, greater statistical suppression by aggression in Sample 2 appeared to obscure the effect of exploitativeness.

Second, there were 41 participants who did not perceive the merchants as credible human co-players (i.e., mean credibility rating of 0 across merchants), and the presence of these participants further attenuated the association.
When we excluded these 41 participants and removed aggression from the model, exploitativeness significantly predicted cheap talk behavior in Sample 2 ( = 0.14, 95% β CI [0.01, 0.27], p = 0.02).
Finally, we pooled data from all three samples to test whether antagonism facets moderated cheap talk while accounting for sample differences.
Before estimating structural effects, we examined measurement invariance of the three-factor antagonism model across Samples 1, 2, and 3 using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (N = 1,533).

The unconstrained confirmatory factor analysis for our 3-factor latent trait model (i.e., configural model) demonstrated acceptable fit ( 2 (186) = 824.83, p < 0.001, CFI = χ 0.92, RMSEA = 0.08, SRMR = 0.06).

Sample was represented by two between-person dummy-coded covariates, and the model retained the progression controls used in the sample-specific analyses.

Our findings suggest that cooperation may reflect not only altruistic motives but also strategic efforts to signal one's cooperativeness to others.

Across three independent samples, participants selectively increased their willingness to cooperate when doing so carried no monetary cost but could plausibly influence their partner's future behavior.
Although return behavior varied with investor reciprocity, the magnitude of cheap talk did not reliably differ across investor types.
Moreover, cheap talk increased both within and across investor interactions, consistent with learning.

Together, these findings challenge the assumption that cooperative behavior necessarily reflects prosocial preferences, instead demonstrating that individuals can learn to express cooperativeness strategically to influence others.
Our findings complement evolutionary and economic accounts of cooperation as a conditional and forward-looking strategy (McNally et al., 2012; McNally & Jackson, 2013; Thöni & Volk, 2018).
text.formatted: Our findings complement evolutionary and economic accounts of cooperation as a conditional and forward-looking strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(McNally et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">McNally & Jackson, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Thöni & Volk, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, most experimental paradigms confound strategic social signaling with reinforcement history or intrinsic prosocial motivation.

By introducing situations in which cooperative signals were both cost-free and nonbinding (i.e., they did not require participants to actually return an investment), our experiment isolated a behavioral signature that is difficult to explain in terms of payoff maximization or learned value alone.

Participants selectively increased cooperative signaling only in contexts where doing so could plausibly affect their partner's future decisions -a pattern consistent with strategic social signaling rather than a stable preference for cooperation.
Conceptually, this resembles game-theoretic cheap talk: cost-free, nonbinding communication that can nevertheless influence another player's beliefs or behavior (Farrell & Rabin, 1996).
text.formatted: Conceptually, this resembles game-theoretic cheap talk: cost-free, nonbinding communication that can nevertheless influence another player's beliefs or behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Farrell & Rabin, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The key difference is that in our task, the signal was behavioral rather than verbal: participants indicated that they would have returned an investment even after the merchant had already kept.
Thus, unlike ordinary reciprocal cooperation, cheap talk is valuable only insofar as it alters the counterpart's expectations or future choices.
We found that strategic cooperation varied across facets of antagonism.
In line with our hypotheses, exploitativeness positively predicted cheap talk in Samples 1 and 3 and in the combined dataset, although evidence was weaker in Sample 2.

This pattern is consistent with prior work linking exploitativeness to enhanced social-cognitive abilities, including theory of mind and social learning, and supports a view of exploitativeness as reflecting a capacity to use social information and social behavior instrumentally (Allen et al., 2017 (Allen et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with prior work linking exploitativeness to enhanced social-cognitive abilities, including theory of mind and social learning, and supports a view of exploitativeness as reflecting a capacity to use social information and social behavior instrumentally <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Allen et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, cooperation may serve as one of several tools through which exploitative individuals shape the behavior of others to advance their own interests.

Conversely, aggression showed a relatively consistent negative association with cheap talk, predicting reduced cooperative signaling in Samples 1 and 3 and in the combined dataset, although not in Sample 2.
This contrast with exploitativeness suggests that these traits may reflect distinct strategies for navigating social interactions.

Whereas exploitative individuals may use cooperative signals instrumentally to encourage favorable treatment, aggressive individuals may be more inclined to respond antagonistically to perceived noncooperation rather than attempting to cultivate future cooperation.
Evidence for callousness was considerably weaker.
Callousness predicted reduced cheap talk in Sample 2 but not in Samples 1 or 3, and its negative association in the combined dataset was small and uncertain.

Importantly, cooperative signaling need not always reflect selfish intentions; it may also serve prosocial goals, such as encouraging others to cooperate and establishing mutually beneficial relationships.
Greater cheap talk among less aggressive individuals may reflect a preference for cooperative rather than conflict-oriented strategies for influencing others.
Whether a similar tendency characterizes more empathic and compassionate individuals remains uncertain given the inconsistent findings for callousness.
Broadly, our findings clarify why exploitativeness may predict cheap talk rather than mere reciprocity.

In our prior work, exploitative individuals showed stronger default network learning signals and greater behavioral reciprocity, suggesting enhanced sensitivity to a counterpart's cooperation history (Allen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In our prior work, exploitative individuals showed stronger default network learning signals and greater behavioral reciprocity, suggesting enhanced sensitivity to a counterpart's cooperation history <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, that pattern could be explained without invoking a representation of the counterpart's mind: exploitative individuals may simply have learned the counterpart's return rate more efficiently and adjusted their policy based on that rate alone.
The present results make this interpretation less plausible.
On trials in which the investor kept the endowment, returning could not improve the participant's immediate payoff and yielded no new information about the investor's return rate.

Instead, the sensitivity of this behavior to investor reciprocity points to a communicative function: it could lead the reciprocating investor to believe that the participant would return a future investment.
Thus, cheap talk depends not merely on learning what the partner tends to do, but on representing how one's own signal may alter the partner's beliefs, expectations, or future choices.

In this sense, cheap talk provides a bridge between prior findings linking exploitativeness to social reinforcement learning and theory of mind, respectively (Allen et al., 2017 (Allen et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: In this sense, cheap talk provides a bridge between prior findings linking exploitativeness to social reinforcement learning and theory of mind, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Allen et al., 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: The primary methodological contribution of this study is isolating the signaling component of cooperative behavior.
By manipulating the cost and long-term return on cooperation, our task differentiates cooperation motivated by immediate incentives from that intended to influence others.

This distinction matters because many cooperative acts are behaviorally identical but psychologically different: the same choice may reflect direct payoff maximization, prosocial motivation, or an attempt to shape a partner's future behavior.
Several limitations should be noted.

First, although participants were led to believe they were interacting with real partners, the use of simulated agents introduces uncertainty about how strongly participants engaged with the social aspects of the task.
Second, our measure of cheap talk necessarily infers strategic intent from patterns of behavior rather than assessing it explicitly.
As such, our design cannot determine whether cheap talk was motivated by the monetary value of influencing the partner, by a desire to appear cooperative to the partner or oneself, or by both.
Third, the assessment of antagonism relied on self-report measures, which is subject to rater biases and may not fully capture the trait's behavioral manifestations.

In sum, the present study demonstrates that cooperation is sometimes used strategically to influence others, and that this tendency constitutes one of the behavioral manifestations of trait exploitativeness.
Our findings characterize cooperation as a flexible social tool that can be deployed in the service of diverse goals.

More broadly, our findings suggest that the social-cognitive capacities that support human cooperation also allow cooperation to be used as a means of influence, and that individuals with greater social-cognitive ability may be most likely to use it this way.
